children.text: A seaside promenade running about 780m along the waterfront on the east side of downtown Dumaguete. It makes a city walking route you can cover on foot in a single day, taking in the sunrise over the sea, the 1903 Silliman Hall, the belfry and cathedral, breakfast fare at the public market, and evening tempura stalls.
Rizal Boulevard is a seaside promenade that runs along the eastern waterfront of downtown
Dumaguete
, at the southeastern tip of Negros Island, from Dumaguete Port in the north toward Pantawan Park in the south. According to a marker put up by the city, it was built in
and is about

long. On the sea side runs a walkway of red bricks laid in a herringbone pattern, along with a stone seawall and old-style street lamps, while across the street stand cafes, restaurants, bars, and hotels set in renovated old mansions. The marker describes the boulevard as "Dumaguete's showcase."
The name comes from José Rizal, the national hero of the Philippines. In

, when the ship carrying Rizal away after his exile in Dapitan stopped at Dumaguete, he is said to have spent a few hours on this shore, before the boulevard existed. At the north end of the boulevard is Dumaguete Port, with boats to Siquijor, Bohol, and Cebu, and just south of it the campus of Silliman University, founded in

by American Presbyterian missionaries, faces the sea. The belfry, which began as a pirate watchtower, St. Catherine of Alexandria Cathedral, the civic square Quezon Park, and the public market all lie within
10–15 minutes
on foot, so downtown is easy to explore in a single walking loop.

The boulevard faces the sea to the east. That means the sun rises over the water, while in the evening it sets behind the mountains at the back of the city. On clear days you can see the southern tip of Cebu Island and Siquijor Island across the sea, and locals gather to jog and stroll from before sunrise. In the evening the street lamps come on, and the boulevard grows busy again with students and families perched on the seawall and crowds around the tempura stalls toward Pantawan in the south.
The boulevard is still changing. In

, a "Smart City" plan was proposed to reclaim about 174 hectares of sea off the boulevard and build an artificial island, but it was halted the same year amid fierce opposition from Silliman University, the Catholic diocese, marine scientists, and residents. At the southern end, the Pantawan area has been expanded by reclamation since
to create Pantawan People's Park; over permit issues, an environmental group filed complaints with the Ombudsman against the mayor and city officials in
, and in
March 2025

coastal protection work followed, widening the promenade and placing wave-breaker blocks. With no entrance fee and flat ground that anyone can walk easily, it suits travelers staying in Dumaguete for a day or more, as well as those with half a day to spare while traveling to and from Siquijor or Apo Island.
The boulevard faces the sea to the east, so the sun rises over the water. Sunrise comes around
depending on the season, and the sky is at its most beautiful in the
20–30 minutes
before the sun comes up. Start your day walking the brick walkway among the jogging locals.

blocks.title: Silliman Hall and the university campus

children.text: Silliman Hall, the white wooden building on the north side of the boulevard, was completed in

as Silliman University's first building and is considered the oldest surviving American-style building in the Philippines. You can pass through the Gate of Opportunity, the old main gate facing the boulevard, and walk around the campus in the shade of big trees.

Located on the second floor of Hibbard Hall on campus, it displays folk artifacts from Negros and the Visayas, as well as old trade ceramics that arrived from Southeast Asia and China. It moved here from Silliman Hall in
, and admission is
for general visitors and
for students.
The stone belfry (Campanario) beside Quezon Park began as a watchtower built to keep watch for Moro pirates while the church was being constructed in
, and bells were added in the late
19th century
; it is a designated Important Cultural Property. Right next to it, St. Catherine of Alexandria Cathedral is known as the oldest stone church on Negros Island.

A downtown square spreading out in front of the belfry and cathedral, centered on an octagonal bandstand with big shade trees and benches. In the evenings it fills with locals and students playing basketball and strolling, and the street parade of Sandurot, the city festival, also ends here.

blocks.title: Morning at the public market's painitan

children.text: About
5 minutes

on foot west of Quezon Park, the painitan inside the public market is an early-morning food alley. A Dumaguete-style breakfast pairs budbud kabog, a millet cake wrapped in banana leaves and steamed, with sikwate, a thick hot chocolate made by melting tablea cacao blocks.
From around
, stalls line up toward Pantawan at the southern end of the boulevard. Dumaguete's tempura isn't Japanese tempura but fried fish cake on skewers, about
per skewer, dipped in a vinegar sauce whose spiciness you choose. Kwek-kwek (battered quail eggs) and balut are sold too.
Started in

in a corner of a family home, the bakery Sans Rival became famous nationwide for silvanas, cookies made of buttercream sandwiched between cashew meringue layers. In an old family mansion on the boulevard is Sans Rival Bistro, opened in
, where you can enjoy cakes and meals while looking out at the sea.

items.title: Half-day morning route
items.subtitle: Sunrise, market breakfast, cathedral, and university

children.text: Watch the sun rise over the sea from the boulevard in front of Silliman Hall. In
December–March
the sun rises around
, so head out a little later.
Walk south along the boulevard to Pantawan People's Park. It takes about
10–15 minutes
, and you'll see the widened seaside promenade and its sculptures.
Head west to the painitan at the public market for a breakfast of budbud kabog and sikwate.
Pass through Quezon Park to see the belfry and St. Catherine of Alexandria Cathedral. If Mass is underway, watch quietly from the back.
Walk
10–15 minutes
north into Silliman University to see Silliman Hall and the campus, then visit the anthropology museum in Hibbard Hall.
Head back out to the boulevard and wrap up with silvanas and coffee at Sans Rival.

The anthropology museum opens mainly on weekdays and closes over lunch, and on Sundays and public holidays you can visit only with an advance reservation. It's safest to schedule this route for Monday to Friday.
Walk beneath the big shade trees of the Silliman University campus, and take photos at the old main gate on the boulevard side and in front of Silliman Hall.
Take a break with silvanas and a drink at Sans Rival Bistro. Frozen silvanas for gifts are best bought on the day you leave.
Walk slowly south from the port area at the north end of the boulevard. The sun sets behind the mountains, so aim for the
20–30 minutes
at dusk when the sky over the sea turns pink.
Have a light dinner of skewers and kwek-kwek at the tempura stalls toward Pantawan.
Relax at a cafe or bar across the boulevard, then take in the illuminated Silliman Hall and belfry before heading back to your lodging.
Stall locations around Pantawan may shift because of construction and events. If you can't spot the stalls, ask people nearby where they sell "tempura."
Cebu Pacific and PAL Express fly nonstop from Manila to Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT), taking about
1 hour 20 minutes
. There are also small-plane routes from Cebu, but flights are few.
The airport is in Sibulan, about
3–5km
north of downtown as the crow flies (the road is longer). A tricycle to the boulevard takes about
20–40 minutes
depending on traffic and costs about
after haggling. If you have large luggage, a hotel pickup or a taxi is more convenient.
Dumaguete Port sits right at the north end of Rizal Boulevard, so from the boat it's only
5–10 minutes
on foot to the boulevard in front of Silliman Hall.
From Siquijor, the OceanJet fast ferry takes about
50 minutes–1 hour
, and as of
July 2026
fares are
for tourist class and
for business class; an October 2026 listing shows tourist class at about ₱350, so fares move with the fuel surcharge.
From Cebu, OceanJet takes about
4 hours 20 minutes
via Tagbilaran, Bohol, and costs about
, or
if you board in Tagbilaran. Fuel surcharges often change fares and schedules, so check the latest notices.

children.text: From Cebu South Bus Terminal, Ceres buses run to Liloan (Santander) port at the southern tip of Cebu Island in about
4–5 hours

From Liloan port, a RoRo ferry crosses to Sibulan port on the Negros side in about
30 minutes
for about

items.title: Getting around town and on foot

children.text: Rizal Boulevard, Silliman University, Quezon Park, the belfry, and the public market are all roughly
10–15 minutes
apart on foot, so you can get around mostly by walking.
As of
March 2026
, the minimum tricycle fare is
per ride, and drivers have been demanding an increase to
. There are no meters, so agree on the fare before you get in.
Since
July 2026
, you can book tricycles through the Maxim app, which shows the fare before you ride.
December–May
is the dry season with little rain, good for walking. In
December–February
the sea breeze is cool enough for daytime strolls, while
March–May
is the hottest but brings clear skies and great sunrise photos. The midday sun is strong, so plan downtown walks for early morning and after
June–November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, and in
July–October
typhoons sometimes cancel boats to Siquijor and Cebu. All-day rain is uncommon, so morning walks are usually possible, but on days with high waves, spray splashes over the seawall.
On
, the provincial government held a dragon boat race off the boulevard, drawing more than 500 paddlers from across the country. In
October
Negros Oriental's provincial festival, Buglasan, takes place, and the city festival, Sandurot, is held in
September
or
November
. Sandurot's dates have shifted from year to year, so check city hall announcements. Around
November 25
, the feast of St. Catherine, the cathedral area is crowded with the city fiesta.

Staying downtown along the boulevard and around Silliman University puts everything from sunrise walks to evening stalls within walking distance. Options range from sea-view hotels on the boulevard to guesthouses and hostels tucked down side streets, at about
per night on booking sites, with the downtown average around
. If diving is your main goal, staying at a dive resort on the
Dauin
coast to the south and visiting the boulevard for a day means less travel.

For food, choose by time of day. Breakfast is budbud kabog and sikwate at the public market's painitan, and for lunch, the inexpensive student eateries around Silliman University or a carinderia where you pick dishes to go with rice are good choices. For dinner, have tempura skewers at the stalls at the south end of the boulevard, or enjoy seafood and Western food at restaurants and bars set in renovated old mansions across the street. For dessert, Sans Rival's silvanas, made since
, are the signature treat, and many people buy frozen silvanas as gifts.
Sunrise is around
in
April–November
and around
in
December–March
. The evening sun sets behind the mountains, so instead of a sunset over the sea, capture the sky over the water as it turns pink.
The boulevard is about
from end to end, or
15–20 minutes
at a leisurely pace. Continuing south to Pantawan Park makes the walk a little longer.
The anthropology museum is on the second floor of Hibbard Hall. Older guidebooks that place it in Silliman Hall reflect information from before
. It closes over lunch and requires a reservation on Sundays and public holidays, so inquire in advance.
The painitan is liveliest around
. Arrive late and many stalls will have run out of budbud kabog.
Many tempura stalls let you choose the spice level of the sauce. Start with a mild level, and buy skewers from stalls that fry them to order.
Many tricycles and stalls accept cash only. Bring plenty of
and
bills.
Silliman University is a working school with classes in session. Follow the instructions of the guards at the main gate, and do not enter classroom or dormitory buildings.
When visiting the belfry and cathedral, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and do not use flash photography during Mass.
Silvanas are kept frozen, so if you have a long trip ahead, ask for insulated packaging.

The Pantawan area at the south end of Rizal Boulevard is reclaimed land where coastal protection work is ongoing, so the promenade and stall locations may change and some sections may be closed off. The reclamation has long been controversial, so do not enter construction zones, and check the latest notices from the City of Dumaguete.
Do not stand on the seawall or sit on its seaward edge to take photos. On days with high waves, spray washes over and makes the ground slippery.
Safety is generally good, but avoid walking alone late at night at the deserted south end of the boulevard or in the market's back alleys, and keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
For street food, choose busy stalls that cook to order, and check that drinks with ice are made with bottled water.
During the typhoon season in
July–October
, boats to Siquijor and Cebu are sometimes canceled, so don't schedule island trips for the day before your flight home.
The unshaded reclaimed sections and the boulevard at midday get very hot. Bring a hat and water, and at midday rest in the shade of the campus trees or indoors.

50 minutes–1 hour
by fast ferry from Dumaguete Port at the north end of the boulevard. A "mystic island" with tiered waterfalls and white-sand beaches.
About

south by bus or jeepney. A muck-diving village where divers seek out seahorses and frogfish.

by car to Malatapay port, then
